【3】**3.5.1 Clinical symptoms and neuropathological findings**

【4】**Contrary to PD， in MSA the alphasynuclein protein displays abnormal depositions mainly in astrocytes (not so much in neurons) and is concen-trated in areas of the autonomic nervous system (peripheral and central). Within a few years， patients develop rapidly progressing balance， speech， and coordination abnormalities . The clinical diagnosis of MSAisnot very predictive of the postmortem-validated diagnosis. A recent study comparing MSA with the results of postmortem neuropathological examinations found that only 62% of the patients suffered from MSA and more than one-third from another disease. The misdiagnosed patients suffered from LBD， PSP， and PD. An incorrect diagnosis of MSA frequently occurs during the first visit (~40%). However， the likelihood of a correct diagnosis increases with the number of visits—up to 92% for patients with a probable MSA and 63%for patients with a possible MSA.**

【5】**Cognitive deficits have been an exclusion criterion for the diagnosis of MSA， however， during the last decades， it has been revealed that MSA patients may suffer from cognitive deficits from the beginning. The same negative statement holds true for visual hallucinations， which are crucial for the diagnosis of LBD. More recent studies have shown that visual hallucina-tion may also be present in MSA patients. However， cognitive impairments and visual hallucination are uncommon in MSA patients and， if present， not very severe.**

【24】**3.5.3 Summarv**

【25】**Presenting symptoms of MSA are autonomic nervous system， cerebellar， and dysarthric disorders. They may also suffer from REM sleep behavioral disor-der. 【27】**3.6Visuoperceptive， visuoconstructive impairments， and visual hallucinations in typical and atypical Parkinson's syndromes**

【28】**We can summarize this chapter by stating that visual hallucinations and delusional misidentifications are a characteristic feature of LBD (and PD)； patients with LBD have severe visuoperceptive problems and tend to neglect global configurational patterns which results in increased false positives to small features of spatial configurations. PD patients undergo similar pro-blems， however， to a lesser extent than LBD patients. Hence suffering from visual hallucinationsSand visuoperceptive impairments correlate in these patient groups. This suggests either a common cause for both symptoms or causation of one symptom for the other. A combination of visuoperceptive impairment and decline of EF could be a prominent explanation for the risk of developing visual hallucinations in PD .**

【29】**However， atypical PD patients， those suffering from PSP or CBD， can also disclose severe impairments with respect to EFs. Yet these atypical PD patients usually do not hallucinate. Moreover these patients have visuoper-ceptive impairments. Fiorenzato et al. 通用删除7(英):<u>(2019)</u> compared 35 PSP patients with Richardson'ssyndrome with130 MSA PD patients. Fiorenzato et al. 通用删除7(英):<u>(2019)</u> followed up about one-half of these groups for a period of 188 months and found that PSP patients were more globally impaired in neuropsychological tests (Montreal Cognitive Assessment， word fluency tasks， Stroop test) as well as in visuoperceptive tasks. The follow-up showed that EFs and judgment of line orientation declined faster in PSP patients than in PD and MSA patients， however， the impairment regarding the incomplete letters test of the VOSP was stable. This would argue that other visuoperceptive tests are related to disease progression in PSP patients as well as in LBD and PD patients. This is especially true for the two latter diseases because LBD and PD patients tend to hallucinate.**

**Bak， Caine， Hearn， and Hodges 通用删除7(英):<u>(2006)</u> compared MSA， PSP， and CBD patients with healthy controls using subtests from the VOSP. CBD/CBS patientsSwere impaired in all VOSP subtests. Patientswith PSP were impaired in number location， dot counting， and silhouette naming. Patients with MSA were not impaired in any of the tests. Ideomotor apraxia， a highly sensitive and specific symptom of CBD/CBS， can be caused by a storage dis-order for the meaning of gestures or action. However， ideomotor apraxia can also be a consequence of a visuoperceptive disorder. This is always the case if the testing comprises meaningless hand positions. During this task， the|删除0换行|visual processing of the hand position of the examiner has to be transformed into the proper visuospatial position of the patient’s hand. If the visuospatial matching of visual to motor coordinates is no longer possible， the patient will fail in this task. Thus visuoconstructive impairments are characteristic features of CBD/CBS patients.**

【31】**Going back to the series of studies published by Mori et al. 通用删除7(英):<u>(2000)</u>， Uchiyama et al. 通用删除7(英):<u>(2012)</u>， and Yokoi et al. 通用删除7(英):<u>(2014)</u>， we can see that in LBD patients visual impairment concerns size and form discrimination and over-lapping figures from the BORB ， object decision from the VOSP ， andface recognition but only inconsistently position discrimination and dot counting . Moreover LBD patients have difficulties responding to local features of figural configurations and not so much to the global features. On the other hand， organizing the different subtests according to the percentage of impaired patients from the Bak et al. 通用删除7(英):<u>(2006)</u> study， clarifies that the impair-ments of PSP and CBD/CBS patients predominantly involve the dot count-ing， the number location， and the cubes tasks from the VOSP. Thus patients with PD or LBD seem to be impaired in visuoperceptive tasks concerning object perception， whereas PSP and CBD/CBS patients seem to be impaired in visuoperceptive tasks concerning object localization and matching spatial coordinate systems of vision and action. Patients with CBD/CBS are often impaired in sensory discrimination and show signs of optic ataxia. Optic ataxia refers to the inability to use visual information to sufficiently guide the hand in the direction of the objects during grasping tasks ， that is， a task for testing object location.**

**Patients with semantic dementia (SD) also show visuoperceptive impair-ments with the core symptom of visual object agnosia. These patients have problems identifying objects， however， they do not suffer from problems in copying them. The explanation for visual object agnosia in these patients may differ from that of patients suffering from classical visual agnostic. Classical visual agnosia is most likely due to a disconnection between visual perception and the stored meaning of objects， whereby the latter is， at least partly， attributable to a degeneration of neuronal repertoires storing the meaning. Furthermore patients with SD do not hallucinate during the early and middle stage of their disease. SD is related to left anterior temporal lobe atrophy. A study from Chan et al. 通用删除7(英):<u>(2009)</u> that compared patients with similar right temporal lobe atrophy with SD patients， revealed that the former patient groups sometimes presented visual hallucination and more behavioral disor-ders. However， one problem with this study was that the right temporal lobe patient groups was selected based on abnormal MRI scans and the amount of|删除0换行|atrophy was significantly higher than in the semantic demented group. Therefore the somewhat increased risk of visual hallucination may be caused by more focal atrophy or due to a later stage of the disease progress.**

【74】**Pediatric seizure syndromes**

【75】**·Seizures are a common occurrence in childhood.**

【76】**·The etiology and appearance of seizures differs based on age of presentation.**

【77】**·A first nonfebrile seizure merits work-up， including laboratory， neuro exam， EEG， and imaging， if indicated.**

【78】**· Provoking factors should be sought， including toxic and metabolic abnormalities (hypoglycemia， electrolyte disturbances， drug ingestions，etc.).**

【79】**·Work-up for a simple febrile seizure may be abbreviated， unless there is an initial suspicion of meningitis/encephalitis， in which case lumbar puncture should be performed. Children with CNS infection will generally have altered mentation.**

【80】**· There are more self-limited， benign types of seizures in children than in adults (i.e. febrile seizures， benign Rolandic epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes，etc.).**

【81】**·There are also more catastrophic epilepsy syndromes in children， and these are associated with intractability and developmental impairment.**

【92】**INTRODUCTION**

【93】The human pituitary is an oval， bean-shaped， and bilaterally symmetric organ located in the sella turcica， near the hypo-thalamus and optic chiasm， surrounded by the sphenoid bone， and covered with the sellar diaphragm. It is a composite endo-crine organ divided in two parts： the adenohypophysis， which derives from an evagination of stomodeal ectoderm (Rathke pouch)， and the neurohypophysis， which arises from the neu-roectoderm of the floor of the forebrain. The adult pituitary weighs about 0.6 g and measures about 13 mm transversely， 9mmanteroposteriorly， and 6mm vertically. Areduction in weight is evident in old age， and an increase occurs during pregnancy andlactation. Althoug h the pituitary size regresses after cessa-tion of lactation， the reversion is notcomplete， the gland weigh-ing 1 g or more in multiparous women.

【94】The adenohypophysis (anteriorlobe) comprises approx 80%of the entire pituitary and includes the pars distalis (PD)， the pars intermedia (PI)， and the pars tuberalis (PT). It produces six distinet hormones， including the three amino acid hormones—growth hormone (GH)， prolactin (PRL)， and adrenocorticotropin(ACTH)—as well as the three glycoprotein hormones—thyro-tropin or thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)， follicle-stimulat-ing hormone(FSH)，andluteinizing hormone (LH). Collectively， these affect the function of virtually all cells in the body 通用删除6(英):<u>\[1\]</u>. Our perceptions of the functional anatomy and cytology of the human pituitary gland underwent considerable change in the last three decades of the 20th century. The enduring concept of the human adenohypophysis comprising five cell types irre-versibly committed to produce six hormones gradually gave way to anew paradigm. In the course ofwork aimed at develop-ing a morphological classification of pituitary adenomas， three distinct tumor types not related to any of the five known cell types were recognized. This finding suggested the existence of three previously unrecognized cell types. Two of these appeared to produce pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)， the prohormone shared by anterior lobe corticotrophs and cells of the PI， thus challenging the assumption that the human PI is vestigial and lacks functional significance. 【1】**5.6 The “Negative” Ultrasound Examination**

【2】**Not infrequently the result of examination is deemed “negative." This means that neither an inflamed appendix nor any other causative condition can be demonstrated by US. In these patients， especially if they are obese， CT may play an important role.**

【3】参考段删除-1:<u>**Early acute appendicitis may be detected by direct visualization of the inflamed appendix or by demonstration of subtle changes in the pericaecal fat  .**</u>

【4】**In patients with a suspected appendiceal mass and equivocal US findings， CT is of paramount importance. It may demonstrate direct-ly the appendiceal phlegmon or abscess but is also capable of detect-ing other conditions . If neither US nor CT study enables a reliable diagnosis to be made， careful clinical expertise re-mains the cornerstone in therapeutic management.**

【5】**Nevertheless， US results may still be of use in these cases. First of all， there may be indirect US findings suggesting the presence of ap-pendicitis . Secondly， in a patient who is easily ex-amined by US and in whom， even after repeated US examinations，no abnormalities are demonstrated， appendicitis， although still possible， is rather unlikely. This information may， to a certain point， influence the therapeutic management. If in such a patient the clinical suspi-cion is high， laparoscopy may provide a useful compromise. Thirdly， if a normal appendix is demonstrated unequivocally， appendicitis may be excluded. It is important then to rule out the pitfalls men-tioned above.**

【11】**Although the appendix may sometimes show “endoappendicitis”when examined microscopically， there is no true obstructive appendi-citis， no imminent perforation， and thus no indication for appendec-tomy. The mural thickening of the terminal ileum and caecum and the enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes provide characteristic US fea-tures， and in fact the use of US in patients with suspected appendici-tis has shed new light on the incidence and the morphological pathol-ogy of this condition， which has turned out to be a very common disease .**

**The clinical features of this otherwise innocuous and self-limiting infection are in most cases indistinguishable from those of appendici-|删除0换行|tis. Clinical clues to the correct diagnosis are a history of a chicken meal， colicky nature of the abdominal pain， and presence of diarrhea. However， in the majority of patients diarrhea is absent or only mild. Those affected include predominantly adolescents and young adults. Campylobacter and Salmonella ileocaecitis usually mimic acute ap-pendicitis， whereas Yersinia ileocaecitis often presents as an appendi-ceal mass. The sedimentation rate is usually elevated in the latter.**

【13】**Bacterial ileocaecitis is the common denominator of many enti-ties in the past described in the literature as， e.g.， Yersinia pseu-doappendicitis， pseudoappendicular syndrome， right iliac fossa syn-drome， bacterial lymphadenitis， acute ileitis， acute terminal ileitis， Yersinia ileitis， Campylobacter-associated appendicitis， barbecue ap-pendicitis， Salmonella pseudoappendicitis， or Salmonella ileocaecal lymphadenitis. Probably many patients treated by appendectomy who have been described as suffering “mesenteric adenitis，”“gastro-enteritis，”or“no abnormalities” have been suffering from unrecog-nized bacterial ileocaecitis .**

【14】**There are several reasons why this common condition has so of-ten gone undetected in the past： (a) In the majority of patients with bacterial ileocaecitis， pain in the right lower abdomen is the predomi-nant symptom， and diarrhea is absent or only mild， so stool cultures are seldom requested. 【65】**6.3.1 Ovarian Cyst**

【66】**The most frequent gynecological condition seen is the persistent and/or hemorrhagic functional cyst， which occurs not only at or a short time after the expected ovulation (intermenstrual pain)， but also later on in the menstrual cycle. 【32】**_A 19-year-old female dance student walks into clinic complaining of intermittent_ _palpitations. She has had four episodes in the last month， each lasting 5 min. 【33】**Palpitations are an unpleasant awareness of the forceful， rapid and/or irregular beating of the heart. It may be due to both cardiac and non-cardiac disease. Most cases are benign， but there are a number of potentially life-threatening arrhythmias. A rational decision-making strategy is needed to quickly identify patients with life-threatening arrhythmias， then risk stratify and determine which patients require advanced investi-gations .**

【34】**A. Unstable Tachyarrhythmias**

【35】**Some arrhythmias can cause haemodynamic instability. First assess the patient for hypotension or serious signs or symptoms (e.g.， drowsiness， shortness of breath， chest pain， syncope). An unstable tachyarrhythmia may require urgent intervention， usually cardioversion.**

【39】**Two key differentiators are 通用删除7(英):<u>(1)</u> is rhythm regular or irregular， and 通用删除7(英):<u>(2)</u> is the QRS complex narrow or wide (normal=80-120 ms=2-3 small squares). The QRS width is the time taken for the complex to reach all ventricular myocardium. An impulse originating from or above the atrioventricular (AV) node， and going down the rapid conducting system， has a short conduction time and narrow QRS width； conversely， QRS is wide in a complex that originates in the ventricles and is not conducted through the rapid conducting system， or if there is a defect in the conducting system. (Note： patients with pacemakers are not discussed in this chapter).**

【66】**Premature beats： May present with palpitations. These tend to occur suddenly and last for no more than an instant.**

【67】**· Premature ventricular contraction (PVC)： A wide QRS complex， not preceded by P wave， followed by a T wave in the opposite direction， and then a compensatory pause. Isolated PVCs are common and do not require further workup. If frequent， consider ambulatory monitoring to determine the frequency and morphology of PVCs， and evaluation for an underlying aetiology-cardiac (hypertensive heart disease， myocardial infarction， heart failure) and non-cardiac disease (caffeine， COPD， hyperthyroidism， etc.).**

【68】**· Premature atrial contraction (PAC)： A premature P wave triggering a normal or aberrant QRS complex. Isolated PACs are common and do not require further workup. If frequent， consider workup to rule out underlying structural heart disease.**

【70】**Structural cardiac abnormalities： Q waves (old infarction)， left ventricular hyper-trophy (structural heart disease and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy) suggest that an arrhythmia may be the cause of palpitations. Attempts to capture the arrhythmia should be pursued .**

【72】**Brugada pattern： Coved ST segment elevation>2 mm， followed by a negative T wave， in more than 1 anterior lead (V1-V3). If symptomatic， this is associated with VT， AF and sudden cardiac death.**

【89】**E. Consider Extended ECG Monitoring**

【90】**Many arrhythmias are intermittent， and may not be captured on a single 10-second ECG. The ECG is more likely diagnostic if captured when the patient has ongoing pal-pitations (e.g.， in an emergency department setting). If an initial ECG is normal， the next decision is whether to pursue extended ECG monitoring. This would depend on the clinical suspicion of an arrhythmia (especially a malignant one).**

【91】**Suggest extended monitoring in patients with：**

【92】**__ Severe symptoms (syncope， chest pain， diaphoresis) during episodes of arrhythmia.**

【93】**Known structural heart disease including ischaemic heart disease， valvular heart disease， cardiomyopathies.**

【94】**__ Family history of sudden cardiac death.**

【95】**Abnormal physical examination， including murmurs， heart failure， displaced apex beat.**

【96】**_Abnormal rest ECG._**

【4】Definition The phenotype of the DiGeorge syndrome(OMIM 188400) was first described in 1965 by Angelo DiGeorge. In the 1990s， it was found that more than90% of individuals diagnosed with the DiGeorge syn-drome have a deletion or microdeletion of the long arm of chromosome 22 (locus 22q11.2). The same genetic defect also has been successively demonstrated in other conditions featuring craniofacial and cardiac defects， such as velocardiofacial syndrome and the conotrun-cal anomaly face. This is why today all of these pheno-types are considered as various expressions of the same genetic anomaly： 22q11 microdeletion.

【5】Etiology and pathogenesis. The various phenotypes are due to microdeletions in the 22q11.2 locus. In over80% of cases， a 3 Mb region between two repeated sequences (low copy repeats or LCRs) on chromosome22 is deleted. The frequency of the defect is due to the fact that， because of the high homology unequal cross-ing-over links occur during meiosis. The recent discov-ery of a rare microduplication 22q11.2 syndrome seems to confirm this pathogenetic mechanism. As mentioned in this chapter the term “microdeletion 22q11.2 syn-drome”encompasses different clinical entities， includ- _ing DiGeorge syndrome， Shprintzen (velo-cardio-facial)_ _syndrome， and Takao (conotruncal anomaly face) syn-_ drome. In particular the phenotypic expression of the22q11.2 microdeletion is extremely variable， though in most cases， cardiac conotruncal defects， thymus hypo-plasia or aplasia， parathyroid hypoplasia or aplasia， and anomalies of the palate are associated with minor cra-niofacial anomalies. All of these malformations involve anatomic structures developing from the third and the fourth pharyngeal arches. The underlying defect consists of an arrest in the development and migration of neural crest cells toward the pharyngeal arches 通用删除6(英):<u>\[10\]</u>.

【6】Genetics. A deletion involving the locus q22.1 on chro-mosome 22 is present in over 90% of the cases. This lesion is rarely so large as to show up on G-banded chromosomes； this happens in only 15%-20% of cases. In most cases， to reveal the microdeletion， a FISH analysis is needed. Several manufacturers have been producing kits for FISH diagnosis of the 22q11microdeletion (Vysis， Oncor etc.). These kits are based on DNA probes for the locus that is usually deleted in this condition，22q11.2. The commercial availabil-ity of these kits has allowed prenatal diagnosis of the Ity22q11 microdeletion. This test is now recommended in those fetuses in which a conotruncal anomaly is found 通用删除6(英):<u>\[11，12\]</u>. In a very limited number of cases， the22q11 microdeletion syndrome may be due to other chromosomal defects， such as a 10p13 monosomy or an 18q21.33 deletion. In these cases also， it has been speculated that genes involved in the neural cell migra-tion process may be deleted. Finally， it is interesting to note that some teratogens (e.g.， retinoic acid deriva-tives) and maternal insulin-dependent diabetes may induce a DiGeorge-like phenotype.

【6】Clinical

【7】 Posterior urethal valves occur only in boys. The exact embryologic abnormality is not known.

【8】 Oliguria can result in utero and produce oligohydram-nios and pulmonary hypoplasia.

【9】 Infants with abnormal prenatal urinary tract findings can be assessed postnatally with fluoroscopic vesico-ureterography (VCUG) and urinary tract sonography. The diagnosis of PUVs should also be considered in a newborn boy with a poor urine stream, a constantly full urinary bladder, multiple urinary tract infections, sepsis, failure to thrive, and nephropathy.

【10】 Unilateral vesicoureteric reflux may be protective of the other kidney. Bladder rupture or calyceal fornix perforation can also occur, causing decompression of the renal collecting system.

【11】 Treatment in utero can be performed using repeated fetal bladder decompression or vesicoamniotic stent placement but has variable results. Postnatal therapy routinely consists of valve ablation via cystoscopy.

【12】 PUVs are responsible for up to 90% of endstage renal disease in boys less than age 4 and accounts for 70% of renal transplantation procedures needed in boys under the age of 5.

【13】Radiologic

【14】 PUVs are best diagnosed on VCUG, on which the valves can balloon out and be visible as a curved filling defect, obstructing the flow of urine from the posterior urethra. The patency of the urethra is maintained posteriorly. The caliber of the anterior urethra is markedly narrowed relative to the distended posterior urethra.

【15】 When assessing the male urethra, three important technical features must be considered to avoid a false-negative examination. First, imaging should be performed after removal of the urinary catheter. Second, the entire urethra must be imaged in a lateral/oblique projection. Third, a large amount of urine must be passing through the urethra at the time of imaging.

【16】 A dilated posterior urethra can be diagnosed using sonography in utero or postnatally; the appearance has been likened to the shape of a “keyhole.”

【17】 In boys with PUVs the appearance of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder is variable; some segments of the urinary tract may be normal. The bladder may have a small luminal capacity, a thick trabeculated hyper-trophied muscle wall and diverticula. One or both ureters may be dilated from obstruction and/or reflux. The kidneys may be hydronephrotic and have dysplastic parenchyma. Sonographically, dysplastic parenchyma typically lacks normal corticomedullary differentiation, has hyperechoic and thinned cortex, and may have associated cysts. Bladder perforation can produce urinary ascites and calyceal perforation can result in peri-nephric urinoma.

【27】DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

【28】 Isolated pulmonic valve stenosis: In this entity, the entirety of blood flow must pass through the lungs. Therefore, the typical finding is a dilated main pulmonary artery and occasionally dilated left pulmonary artery with normal pulmonary blood flow. A decrease in pulmonary blood flow would not be expected in the setting of isolated pulmonic valve stenosis (i.e. in the absence of an intracardiac shunt).

【29】 Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF): The combination of a large subaortic ventricular septal defect (VSD), right ventricular hypertrophy, and small pulmonary arteries is typical of this diagnosis. These findings are all present in the case illustrated, making this the most likely diagnosis. The majority of these patients have a left aortic arch, although 25% have a right aortic arch.

【30】 Pulmonary valve atresia with intact ventricular septum: The presence of cardiomegaly and diminished pulmonary blood flow on the radiographs raises this as a possible diagnosis. However, the presence of a large VSD on the MR scan excludes this diagnosis.

【31】 Ebstein’s anomaly: Patients with Ebstein’s anomaly usually present with cyanosis in the neonatal period and have marked right-sided cardiac chamber enlargement (including both the right atrium and right ventricle) and diminished pulmonary blood flow (as a result of severe tricuspid regurgitation and right-to-left shunting across the atrial septum). This diagnosis is unlikely for two reasons: 通用删除7(英):<u>(1)</u> cardiac size is usually (but not invariably) much larger than shown in Figure 8-16A —in particular, the right heart size is increased in Ebstein’s anomaly but not in the case depicted here; and 通用删除7(英):<u>(2)</u> the MR scan in this case shows an aorta overriding a VSD, not a feature of Ebstein’s anomaly.

【32】 Tricuspid atresia: These patients can present with cardiomegaly and diminished pulmonary blood flow. However, the presence of an otherwise normal, but thick-walled, right ventricular chamber on the MR examination in the case shown makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

【33】DIAGNOSIS

【34】TOF with diminutive pulmonary arteries following central shunt

【35】KEY FACTS

【36】Clinical

【37】 The finding of cyanosis indicates a right-to-left shunt or an admixture lesion.

【38】 TOF can be associated with pulmonic stenosis at any of four levels: the infundibulum (most common), the pulmonic valve, the pulmonary trunk, or the pulmonary artery branches.

【39】 If pulmonary atresia is present, the entire pulmonary blood flow is through collateral (i.e. bronchial) vessels that reach the pulmonary vasculature from the descending thoracic aorta.

【40】 TOF is the most common malformation among cyanotic adults with congenital heart disease.

【41】Radiologic

【42】 The ascending aorta and aortic knob are prominent in TOF because the aorta receives the vast majority of the blood flow from both ventricles.

【43】 Cardiac size in TOF is usually normal because although right ventricular hypertrophy is present, little ventricular dilation is present.

【44】 In the TOF variant, in which there is absence of the pulmonic valve, marked dilatation of the pulmonary trunk and its proximal branches can be seen, frequently resulting in compression of the airway.

【45】 Occasionally, absence of a pulmonary artery branch is seen in TOF, usually involving the side opposite the aortic arch.

【46】 MR imaging can be a useful tool to determine the size of the pulmonary arteries, which is helpful for preoperative planning and evaluation of growth following a palliative procedure (e.g. after a systemic-arterial shunt). MR imaging also allows evaluation of important anatomic details—for example, whether the pulmonary arteries are confluent, which is a factor facilitating surgical repair.

【59】 Anterior mediastinal mass: An anterior mediastinal mass might be suspected because of the frontal chest radiograph findings. However, the lateral radiograph shows that some of the abnormal density is in the posterior mediastinum (as well as the anterior mediastinum), near the location of the left ventricle. The left ventricle enlargement is due to aortic regurgitation. This diagnosis best accounts for the imaging findings.

【61】 Aortic stenosis: The enlargement of the ascending aorta in this case could potentially be due to the jet effect of aortic stenosis. However, at a point at which the aorta is enlarged to the degree shown in the illustrated case, clinical symptoms and signs (e.g. dyspnea, exertional chest pain, syncope, or an apical systolic ejection murmur) would be expected to be quite evident. This diagnosis is incorrect.

【62】DIAGNOSIS

【63】Ascending aortic aneurysm due to Marfan syndrome

【64】KEY FACTS

【65】Clinical

【66】 Aneurysms of the ascending aorta are rare in children but are much more common in adults (in whom the most common etiology is atherosclerotic disease).

【67】 Ascending aortic aneurysms in children are usually due to a genetic disease such as Marfan syndrome, cutis laxa, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, homocystinuria, Noonan’s syndrome, and Turner’s syndrome.

【68】 Marfan syndrome is a disease in which an abnormality of the elastic media is present. The term “cystic medial necrosis” has been used to describe the underlying abnormality; however, the term is a misnomer because necrosis is not present. Other major cardiac anomalies in Marfan syndrome are aortic valve and mitral valve insufficiency as well as dissection of the aneurysm.

【69】 Ehlers-Danlos syndrome represents a group of related collagen disorders in which hyperelasticity and joint laxity are typical clinical features.

【70】 In homocystinuria, mental retardation is typically present, unlike in the case illustrated.

【71】 Osteogenesis imperfecta type 1 is associated with aortic root dilatation. A clinical history of fractures or blue sclera (which are not present in the case illustrated) is typically found.

【72】 Aortic surgery or replacement of the aortic valve or mitral valve is rarely necessary before adolescence in Marfan syndrome. On the other hand, in the adolescent or adult, repair of the ascending aorta usually is performed for an aneurysm of 6.0 cm or greater.

【73】Radiologic

【74】 Plain radiographs are sometimes used as the initial imaging technique for detection of an ascending aortic aneurysm. However, they are insensitive for detection of an aneurysm and have little value in patient assessment.

【75】 Echocardiography is a widely-used noninvasive tool for determining the dimensions of an ascending aortic aneurysm, detecting the presence of valvular regurgitation, and evaluating left ventricular function.

【76】 MR imaging is recommended in patients in whom the acoustic window is limited (including Marfan syndrome, where pectus deformity may limit evaluation, thereby precluding effective use of sonography) and in those with known dilation of the ascending aorta and acute chest pain (in whom aortic dissection is suspected).

【77】 MR imaging for evaluation of an ascending aortic aneu-rysm should be performed using a combination of transaxial, coronal, and sagittal cardiac-gated T1-weighted sequences. Gradient-recalled (so-called bright blood) pulse sequences may also be helpful, particularly in a cine mode.

【78】 Catheter angiography can give much of the same information as MR imaging. However, given the increased risk of aortic injury in a patient with a known aortic aneurysm or suspected dissection, noninvasive imaging techniques are preferred.

【94】For this case, a differential diagnosis can be generated based on either the avascular necrosis or the epiphyseal fragmentation. The differential diagnosis for avascular necrosis of the hip in a child includes the following:

【95】 Sickle cell anemia: Bony changes associated with sickle cell hemoglobinopathies can include sclerosis, “bone-within-bone” appearance in the femurs, and perios-teal reaction (from acute infarction or, less commonly, osteomyelitis). None of those changes are present in the case shown here. Furthermore, the child is Caucasian. This diagnosis is incorrect.

【96】 Trauma: Trauma can produce some of the changes shown in this case. However, no history of trauma is provided, making this diagnosis unlikely.

【97】 Osteomyelitis: Osteomyelitis can cause changes that mimic avascular necrosis. Clinical and laboratory features (including elevation of the sedimentation rate) consistent with infection are typically present. However, no clinical features suggestive of infection are provided in this case, making the diagnosis unlikely. In equivocal cases where infection appears to be a possibility, osteomyelitis can be distinguished from avascular necrosis by a bone scan that showed increased radiotracer activity in all phases of a three-phase scan. This test would be helpful unless mechanical factors related to infection, for example, infectious synovitis, produced decreases in the vascular supply of the femoral head.

【98】 Gaucher’s disease: This entity can produce osteone-crosis but other typical features of Gaucher’s disease, for example, expanded medullary cavities with a thin cortex, osteopenia, and absence of normal metaphyseal widening, are not present in the case shown. This diagnosis is unlikely.

【99】 Legg-Calvé-Perthes (Legg-Perthes) disease: This disease produces deformity of the epiphysis and subchon-dral lucencies due to avascular necrosis and typically occurs in Causcasian boys in the 4 to 8 years age range (consistent with the clinical history in the case presented). This diagnosis is the most likely.

【100】Diagnostic considerations for causes of a fragmented epi-physis include the following:

【101】 Hypothyroidism: This disease produces fragmentation in both femoral heads at the onset of ossification. However, in the case shown, the right femoral head is normal in appearance, making this diagnosis unlikely.

【102】 Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia: This disease produces bilateral, symmetric epiphyseal fragmentation; the fragments often coalesce over time and mimic the coxa magna appearance seen in late Legg-Perthes disease. However, unilateral findings in the case shown here make this diagnosis unlikely.

【103】 Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease: In advanced stages of this disease, fragmentation of epiphyses can occur. Unlike hypothyroidism and multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, findings of Legg-Perthes are usually unilateral, making it a realistic diagnostic possibility in the case presented here. Furthermore, it is the only entity on both differential diagnosis lists (i.e. as a cause of both fragmented epiphyses and avascular necrosis of the hip), making it the most likely diagnosis.

【29】**RECOVERY FROM PSYCHOTIC DISORDERS**

【30】**Benign and transitory psychoses are by their nature time-limited. There are many psychoses that resolve on their own， leaving no trace of their prior ex-istence and creating no adaptational consequences. The psychosis associated with neurodevelopmental disorders， such as Asperger’s syndrome， autism，and others tend to be episodic and stress-related； the same could be said for psycho-sis associated with borderline， multidimensional impairment， and personality disorders. Psychosis symptoms associated with medical conditions， in general， improve when the medical conditions are appropriately treated.**

【31】**In general， the psychoses associated with mood disorders (major depressive episodes and bipolar disorders) are state-related； that is， the psychotic features tend to resurface when the mood disorder is destabilized. Frequently， this is an indicator of noncompliance or of a major adaptational stressor. On the other hand， psychoses associated with schizophrenic spectrum disorders tend to be chronic and are usually severe and incapacitating. Even with the psycho-pharmacological advances in the field of psychosis， schizophrenia spectrum disorders still carry a guarded prognosis. This is more so for very early onset schizophrenia (VEOS) and early onset schizophrenia (EOS)， since the early emergence of these disorders disrupts and deviates psychosocial development and disturbs the optimal adaptation to school and the social milieu.**

【44】** _NIRAVASCULAR_ papillary endothelial hyperplasia and angiosarcoma are both characterized by irregularly shaped， anasto-mnosing， endothelium-lined vascular channels within which papillated， vil-lous-like fronds protrude into the lumina. Other histologic features that these two lesions share are mixed inflammatory-cell infiltrates， sidero-phages， and erythrocytes within the lumina of the vascular spaces. The major differences between the lesions are that intravascular papillary endo-thelial hyperplasias are smaller， are confined within a pre-existing throm-bosed vascular space， and have almost no nuclear atypia. Angiosarcomas are larger， asymmetric， poorly circumscribed， unrelated to an antecedent thrombosed vessel， and may have marked nuclear atypia and mitotic fig- _ures._**

【45】**Intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia is also known as Mas-son’s vegetant intravascular hemangioendothelioma， intravascular angio-matosis， and intravascular hemangioma. It is a histologic rather than a clinical diagnosis， and it presumably results from recanalization of a thrombus. This process takes place in an endothelium-lined structure， such as a hemangioma， a dilated vein or varix， and a pyogenic granuloma. Less frequently， the papillary endothelial hyperplasia occurs within a hematoma. Clinically， Masson’s lesion is a solitary， bluish or reddish， firm nodule. In most instances， it grows slowly and has been present for months or years. Patients may complain that the nodule is painful or tender， The lesion may arise on any area of the body， but the head and neck are most often affected.**

【46】**A Masson’s lesion begins when elongated， spindle-shaped endothelial cells proliferate within a fibrin clot， nearly always situated inside a pre-existing endothelium-lined space. As the fibrin is recanalized by capillaries， small papillae or buds covered by plump endothelial cells， and but one cell thick， form a labyrinth of irregularly-shaped vascular channels. In some areas， the endothelial cells within the fibrin clot probably act as facultative fibroblasts and lay down collagen， which replaces the fibrin. In most lesions of intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia， some fibrin is still visible and all stages in the process are present. In older lesions， however， in which the scenario is complete， no thrombus or fibrin residua are present， only the fully devcloped papillary endothelial hyperplasia. This fact is probably why some students of these lesions have failed to find fibrin and why some came to misinterpret Masson’s lesion as a primary proliferative process rather than merely a recanalizing thrombus.**

Angiosarcoma， also known as malignant hemangioendothelioma， is a malignant neoplasm of'endothelial cells characterized by the formation of|删除0换行|irregularly-shaped vascular spaces lined by atypical endothelial cells. It usu-ally arises on the scalp or face of persons in the seventh or eighth decades of life. Usually bluish or violaceous， these patches， plaques， or nodules are soft， sponge-like， and nonpulsatile. The clinical lesion is usually poorly circum-scribed， roundish or oval， and generally ranges from 1.5 to 4 cm in diareter by the time that it is first examined. The lesion is usually not painful or tender， but bleeding， cither ““spontaneously”or after minor trauma， and ulceration are common complications.**

Many lesions eventually give rise to distant metastases， especially to the cervical lymph nodes and the lungs. One subsct of patients with angiosarcomas is young women， who develop fulminant angiosarcomasparticularly of a breast. Most of these patients suffer wide-spread metastases within one year. 【53】**INTRODUCTION**

【54】Plasmablastic differentiation can be found in a wide range of large B-cell lymphomas， including plasmablastic lymphoma(oral mucosa type)， plasmablastic lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation， primary effusion lymphoma (PEL)； Kaposi’s sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV)-positive solid lymphoma/extra-cavitary PEL/human herpesvirus (HHV)-8 associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)； large B-cell lymphoma aris-ing in HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman’s disease； and DLBCL expressing anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)通用删除6(英):<u>\[1-11\]</u>.

【55】**PLASMABLASTIC LYMPHOMA**

【56】**INTRODUCTION**

Plasmablastic lymphoma is a rare aggressive large B-cell lymphoma composed of large cells with immunoblastic/plas-mablastic features， which usually occurs in HIV+ patients通用删除6(英):<u>\[2-4，6\]</u>. It was originally described in the oral cavity， but it can occur in the lymph nodes， skin， soft tissues， and other extranodal sites. At presentation， 90% of patients have extra-nodal involvement， 69% present with advanced stage disease， and 27% had oral involvement 通用删除6(英):<u>\[12\]</u>. Disseminated presen-tation is not uncommon. The cytomorphologic features resemble“immunoblastic”variant of DLBCL， plasma cell myeloma (PCM) with anaplastic features， precursor B- and T-cell lymphomas， and myeloid neoplasms. Plasmablastic lymphoma may occur as a posttransplant lymphoprolifera-tive disorder (PTLD) 通用删除6(英):<u>\[13\]</u>. Plasmablastic lymphoma is often|删除0换行|associated with MYC-IGH rearrangement 通用删除6(英):<u>\[12，14\]</u>. Castillo reported MYC rearrangement in 41% of patients. The median overall survival is 11 months， regardless of the intensity of chemotherapy 通用删除6(英):<u>\[11，12\]</u>.**

【58】**MORPHOLOGY**

【59】**Typical plasmablastic lymphoma (oral mucosa type) shows diffuse and monotonous infiltrate of large cells with either plasmablastic or immunoblastic morphology . Nuclei are large， oval to round with open chroma-tin and prominent nucleoli. Similar to other high-grade tumors， mitoses， tingible body macrophages， and apoptotic cells are easily identified and many cases show a “starry-sky”pattern. Cases of plasmablastic lymphoma with plasmacytic differen-tiation show variable numbers of cells with plasmacytic differ-entiation and monoclonal light-chain expression .**

【60】**IMMUNOPHENOTYPE**

【61】Plasmablastic lymphomas are strongly positive for CD38， CD138， and MUM1； may be positive for CD10 and CD56； and express Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)/EB V-encoded RNA通用删除1(英):<u>(EBER； Figures 17.1 through 17.4)</u>. They are negative for surface light- and immunoglobulin heavy chains (by flow cytometry)， ALK， CD30， CD45， and CD117. BCL6 expres-sion is variable and mostly negative. CD20 is negative in most cases， but rare cases may show weak staining. Subset of tumors expresses MYC， CD43， and CD79a. Cytoplasmic

【72】**The differential diagnosis includes DLBCL (especially immunoblastic variant)， ALK+large B-cell lymphoma， PEL， extracavitary PEL， large B-cell lymphoma arising in Kaposi sarcoma-associated virus-positive multicentric Castleman’s disease， EMT， poorly differentiated carcinoma， precursor B-ALL/LBL and T-ALL/LBL， and PCM. Positive expression of EBER and lack of CD20， PAX5 (and often other B-cell markers)， CD45， and BCL6 distinguishes plasmablastic lym-phoma from DLBCL (subset of plasmablastic lymphomas may be CD45+， and rare cases of DLBCL may be CD20-).**

Plasmablastic lymphoma and PCM have a very similar phenotype： Both tumors are positive for CD38，CD138，and MUM1； often express CD56； may be positive for CD10； and are negative for CD20 and PAX5 (subset of PCM may|删除0换行|be CD20+ and/or PAX5+， however). Plasmablastic lym-phomas and rare cases of PCM may be CD45+. EBER expression is the major factor in differential diagnosis； it is positive in plasmablastic lymphoma and negative in multiple myeloma (MM； even those with plasmablastic cytomorphology).

【74】Precursor B-ALL/LBL differs by expression of CD19， CD22， CD34， CD45， CD79a， terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT)， and often bright CD10， as well as nega-tive EBER. Precursor T-ALL/LBL differs by positive cyto-plasmic CD3， CD7， CD34， TdT， and negative EBER. Positive keratin distinguishes poorly differentiated carcinomas and positive ALK differentiates ALK+ large B-cell lymphoma and anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL). EMT/acute myeloid leukemia (AML) differs from plasmablastic lym-phoma by expression of CD13， CD15， CD33， CD34， CD117， MPO， CD68， and negative EBER.

【75】A variant of plasmablastic lymphoma may occur in the set-ting of multicentric Castleman’s disease . They occur in the lymph nodes and spleen， and frequently involve the blood. The neoplastic cells form vague nodules that are surrounded by polytypic plasma cells. Lymphomatous cells·have immunoblastic morphology； are positive for CD20(dim)， CD45， HHV-8， and lambda immunoglobulins； and negative for CD30 and EBV.

【76】ENKTL， which is EBVEBER+， is composed of either small， intermediate， or large cells (often shows a mixture of small and large cells) and differs from plasmablastic lymphoma by expression of CD2， cytoplasmic CD3， and cytotoxic markers \[e.g.， T-cell-restricted intracellular antigen(TIA-1)\]. Rare ENKTLs may be CD8+.

【91】**EBV+ LYMPHOPROLIFERATIONS**

【92】EBV-associated lymphoproliferative disease (LPD) is the result of the outgrowth of EBV-infected B cells that would normally be controlled by an effective EB V-specific cyto-toxic T-cell response. LPD may occur during both primary and secondary immune deficiencies and even in some per-sons without documented immunodeficiency.

【93】**EBV is a latent y-herpesvirus that infects >90% of popu-lation. Primary lytic infection occurs in the oropharynx and may be asymptomatic or present as infectious mononucleosis.**

【94】**EBC is highly immunogenic and during primary infection causes a vigorous humoral and cellular immune response. After clearance of primary infection， EBC persists as an episome in infected B cells， establishing latent infection characterized by the expression of only a limited array of subdominant EBV antigens. There are four types of latency， distinguished by the pattern of EBC antigen expression in infected memory cells.**

【95】Most infected circulating memory B cells express no viral antigens (type 0 latency) allowing them to remain invisible to the host immune system. Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen 1(EBNA-1)， which acts on a latent origin of replication， is responsible for coordinating replication of the latent episome. Type I latency is associated with expression of only EBNAl and is seen in circulating B cells when they proliferate and in Burkitt lymphoma (BL). In type II latency， LMPl and LMP2

【1】**Neuroimaging**

【2】**Several recent studies have utilized brain imaging technology to exam-ine whether there are structural and functional abnormalities in CFS patients. Buchwald and colleagues 通用删除7(英):<u>(1992)</u> found significantly more cerebral abnormalities on MRI in CFS patients (78%) vs healthy controls(21%). This finding was replicated by Natelson， Cohen， Brassloff， and Lee 通用删除7(英):<u>(1993)</u> with cerebral abnormalities on MRI observed in 27% of the CFS group compared to 2% of controls with mild head injury or headache. When abnormalities are observed on MRI imaging， they are primarily small white matter hyperintensities， most often in the frontal lobes. However， subsequent studies have failed to reveal group differ~ences between CFS and healthy controls， results that are likely due to small sample size . However， another factor that significantly influences group differences is the het-erogeneity of the CFS sample. Lange and colleagues 通用删除7(英):<u>(1999)</u> reported no differences in cerebral abnormalities between the CFS (46.2%) and healthy (31.6%) groups. However， when the CFS group was partitioned into subjects with vs without psychopathology concurrent with their ill-ness， significantly more abnormalities were observed in the CFS group without psychopathology (66.7%) compared to the CFS group with psy-chopathology (primarily depression： 22.2%) and controls (31.6%). Greco， Tannock， Brostoff， and Costa 通用删除7(英):<u>(1997)</u> reported similar findings by observing no group differences when CFS subjects were combined as a whole. However， when stratified by the presence or absence of psy-chopathology， only the CFS subjects without psychopathology showed cerebral abnormalities compared to healthy controls (p<.06).**

【3】**Regarding functional neuroimaging， several studies have utilized SPECT technology and have reported abnormalities in up to 81% of subjects with CFS . Importantly， some SPECT studies have reported significant differences between CFS subjects and depressed subjects ， but not all . The only SPECT study to stratify CFS subjects into those with and without psy-chopathology  reported similar find-ings to that described above using MRI technology： namely， significantly reduced brainstem hypoperfusion was greatest in CFS subjects without psychopathology.**

【4】**DIFFERENTIATING CFS FROMOTHER FATIGUING CONDITIONS**

【5】**In the sections that follow， the similarities and differences in neuropsy-chological functioning between CFS and other fatiguing illnesses are presented.**

【6】**Comparison of Neuropsychological Functioning in CFS and MS**

【7】**Studies have found that CFS and MS subjects show some similarities in neuropsychological performance . For example， DeLuca and colleagues 通用删除7(英):<u>(1993)</u> found that CFS subjects and individuals with mildly physically disabling MS demonstrated impair-ment on a measure of complex auditory information processing. These findings were replicated by their later workk . Finally， recent evidence suggests that memory impairment in both CFS and MS is due primarily to deficient acquisition or encoding of informa-tion， rather than in consolidation or retrieval from long-term storage.**

**Despite these similarities in performance， individuals with MS suffer from more severe and more widespread neuropsychological impair-ments than do individuals with CFS . Despite significant heterogeneity， individuals with MS have been reported to demonstrate impairments in conceptual reasoning， memo-ry， and visuospatial performance . Aside from memory imoairments， these deficits are|删除0换行|not commonly seen in CFS . Moreover， unlike CFS， MS subjects have been found to demonstrate deficits on measures of both visual and auditory complex information processing .**

【9】**Comparison of Neuropsychological Functioning in CFS， MTBI， and Post-Lyme Syndrome**

【10】**Two other disorders that have clinical presentations similar to CFS are MTBI (i.e.， post-concussive syndrome)；  and post-Lyme syndrome .**

【11】**As in CFS， complaints of cognitive impairment and fatigue are com-mon in MTBI or， more specifically， post-concussive syndrome . Neuropsychologically， deficits in attention/concentra-tion/information processing are hallmark features of both CFS and MTBI. Although the profile of neuropsychological impairment is simi-lar in CFS and MTBI， MTBI subjects demonstrate more severe and per-vasive impairment than do CFS subjects .**

【12】**Post-Lyme disease syndrome is a disorder characterized by cognitive complaints， fatigue， and malaise . The condition follows documented Lyme disease and is therefore best diagnosed medically. With regard to neuropsychological functioning， post-Lyme patients have been found to demonstrate more significant neuropsychological impairment than individuals with CFS . Post-Lyme patients have also been found to demonstrate more significant neuropsychological impairment than individuals with fibromyalgia， a disorder similar to CFS .**

【13】**Comparison of Neuropsychological Functioning in CFS and Gulf War Syndrome**

【14】**Following their return from the Persian Gulf War numerous veterans reported a fatigue-like illness with multiple somatic complaints . These symptomatic veterans， often labeled as suffering from Gulf War Syndrome， have also been found to demon-strate neuropsychological deficits .Overall， the neuropsychological deficits in this population appear to be subtle and may be linked to psychiatric disturbance .**

【15】**However， an estimated 5.1% of Gulf era veterans have been found to have CFS . Thus， some symptomatic Gulf veterans may demonstrate neuropsychological pro-fiies typical of CFS.**

【16】**CONCLUSIONS**

【17】**Our focus in this chapter has been to familiarize the reader with CFS as an illness， and to provide a framework by which CFS can be differentiat-ed from depression. The differential diagnosis between depression and CFS is not a trivial matter because it can affect the focus of therapy and the delivery of services. Moreover， “CFS is certainly not simply the somatic presentation of an affective disorder” . CFS is a heterogeneous illness whose precise definition remains elusive. The polar conceptualization of CFS as either a psychi-atric or a medical illness is simplistic and provides little benefit to the patiert， society， or science.**

【18】**Since many CFS symptoms overlap with depression， differential diagnosis is often a complex process. However， there are soine key fea-tures of each illness to keep in mind when completing a diagnostic evaluation. First， infectious symptoms and a sudden ilness onsei are more characteristics of CFS than of depression. Moreover， although sleep disturbance is common in both disorders， the sleep disorder asso-ciated with depression is carly morning awakening that is often not seen in CFS. Psychological presentation can be a key feature differenti-ating the disorders. Specifically， low mood， feelings of guilt， self-reproach， and an internal illness attribution suggest that a depressive disorder is present. The neuropsychological characteristics of the two disorders are highly similar， with deficits primarily in attention/con-centration and information processing efficiency. Thus， the neuropsy chological evaluation alone may not yield sufficient information for differential diagnosis，**

【19】**Fatigue can be viewed as either a symptom of an illness (e.g.， depression) or as an illness itself (i.e.， CFS). This multidimensional view of fatigue as both a syiptom and an illness often complicates differential diagnosis. As such， a differential diagnostic determina tion based on the symptom of fatigue alone is inappropriate. Fatigue as an illness is a concept that is still evolving and remains， as yet， poor-ly understood.**

【5】**1.6 Structured and efficient testing presupposes a structured and efficient anamnesis**

**The specific strategy of testing patients for a differential diagnosis should be based on a preliminary idea/suspicion of the patient’s disease (whereby this hypothesis should be reformulated if test results are discrepant). The anam-nesis provides the necessary information to formulate a first hypothesis for the testing strategy(. For many patients， one will have to go back to the anamnesis more than once or patients and their relatives must be given questionnaires to validate the etiological hypothesis. An anamnesis should start with patients providing a description of their problems (by them-selves). It is important to ask relatives not to intervene during this phase and to wait with comments and additional information until the anamnesis of the patient is finished. After the spontaneous delineation of the problems， that is， the reasons for attending the neuropsychological assessment， the anamnesis should primarily focus on the functions of the autonomous nervous system. This includes problems with swallowing and speaking (hoarseness)， pro-blems with vertigo， incontinence and constipation， erectile dysfunctions， and any sleep issues (duration， depth， and motor unrest such as speaking during sleep， and restless legs). Disorders of the autonomous nervous system， in situations where they cannot be explained by additional diseases， are fre-quently anindicationforrtypicalOTatypical1Parkinson's disease. Incontinence might be a symptom of normal pressure hydrocephalus. Finally|删除0换行|regularly sleeping 10 or more hours a daycan be aa sign of ongoing neurodegeneration.**

【7】**The anamnesis should then focus on walking impairments， experienced falls， and postural instability as well as the use of the hands， handwriting， and any existing tremor. Resting tremor， frequent falls， problems with pos-tural balance， and limited handwriting abilities are frequent problems in idio-pathic and atypical Parkinson’s disease. The third major topic of the anamnesis concerns the senses， that is， deficits in seeing， hearing， smelling， and taste. Hypoacusis (partial loss of hearing ability) is a common problem in elderly individuals which leads to social isolation and may have detrimen-tal effects on cognition. Therefore advising the patient to use hearing aids the whole day might be helpful. Olfactory deficits may be the first signs of a beginning Parkinson’s disease. Furthermore the patient should be asked about his or her appetite as well as possible weight loss since weight loss is common in patientsVwith dementia. In this case， weight lossis usually accompanied by some loss of appetite or of having a regular meal. A signifi-cant weight loss (>8 kg in less than half a year) without any explanation(e.g.， another disease， voluntary reduction of caloric intake) should be han-dled as a warning signal for a possible cancer or tumor growth.**

【8】**The next step of the anamnesis should focus on the cognitive functions of memory， working memory， attention， and language. Patients with subjective memory impairments should always be asked whether they have problems with orientation in new environments (e.g.， when they are on vacation). The anamnesis should also try to determine whether the subjective memory impairment concerns episodic memory (Can you remember things that you heard yesterday?) or working memory (Do you (only) forget what your intention is when you move into the next room?). Working memory pro-blems are uncommon in Alzheimer’s disease； however， patients often con-fuse them with episodic memory problems. To gain a better impression of the problem， one may also ask whether the patients usually remember the forgotten events through recognition， that is， after receiving some cues about the event by relatives or friends. Intact recognition but high forgetfulness biases the diagnostic hypothesis away from AD.**

【9】**Attentional performance should be assessed by differentiating between distractibility and tiredness. Again， excessive tiredness1LsSunusual for Alzheimer’s disease. Falling asleep during the day may be caused by sleep problems (e.g.， sleep apnea) or by cardiovascular diseases. Both are often associated with cognitive problems. If patients stress that they tire quickly， one should also ask if they experience mental slowing when confronted with problems. Mental slowing is a typical problem in patients with white matter lesions (vascular dementia) as well as in patients with Parkinson’s disease.**

**The questions regarding language impairments concern understanding， word finding problems， and reduced drive for verbal communication. It is important to inquire about comprehension and word finding problems|删除0换行|separately and to make sure that the patients report their verbal understand-ing abilities independent of hearing problems. If the patient reports word finding problems，oneshould examine (as with memory impairments) whether this impairment started suddenly， if it is slowly increasing or if it is constant. Another important question is whether it concerns the speaking or the access of the words. Moreover， it is important to look for paraphasia dur-ing the interaction with the patient. Paraphasia may concern the use of a wrong， but semantically related word or producing phonological similar but deviating words. It is important to note which of these possibilities are pres-ent. Another aspect of language is how the patient’s speech sounds： are there any signs of dysarthric speech or reduction in the force of the voice? If the patients are answering only in short sentences， one should also ask if they have lost interest in or reduced their amount of verbal interactions.**

【11】**The last topic of the anamnesis regarding subjectively experienced changes concerns mood. Questioning patients about mood changes should cover aspects such as depressed or euphoric mood， loss of drive， social with-drawal， increased irritability， anxiety and fearfulness， and being driven by unrest. Feeling more dependent on others is typical for patients with AD， whereas social withdrawal and increased irritability in the presence of stran-gers might be an indication of the behavioral variant of frontotemporal dementia. On the other hand， increased short-term irritability and affect labil-ity are symptoms often associated with vascular dementia. If the patient tries to encourage a relative to answer the questions during the anamnesis， the development of the patient’s interpersonal dependency， for example， a recent aversion of being home alone， should be examined.**

【12】**The last part of the anamnesis concerns the medical history. The patient should be asked about any drugs or medications he or she is taking. The meaning of the question has also been introduced above. It is also important to ask if they have already experienced any neurological， psychiatric or psy-chological disorder， or disease during their life. This question should be broadened to include the medical history of the patient’s family as well. There are some kinds of dementia that have a strong genetic component(e.g.， behavioral frontotemporal lobe dementia， early onset Alzheimer’s dis-ease). Finally， whether the patient has been assessed by cranial Computer Tomography or Magnet Resonance Imaging should be established and the results should be requested.**

**After having finished the anamnesis with the patients， the relatives should be asked whether the patient’s answers fit their impressions or whether there are differences. After discussing potential differences between the patients report and that of the relatives， one should explicitly ask whether the patients suffer from motor unrest during night-time dreaming ， how long they sleep|删除0换行|during the day， whether there is a change in appetite and how the relatives rate the memory performance. Another important topic concerns the rela-tive’s impression of the patient’s mood and behavior. If there are signs of increased irritability and disinhibition， whether the patient is only aggressive at home or whether the patient is also aggressive and/or show aberrant behavior towards strangers should be determined. Relatives should also fill out questionnaires regarding the instrumental abilities of daily living， the neuropsychiatric inventory and whether the patient moves and speaks during sleep as well as a questionnaire concerning REM sleep behavior disorder. These questionnaires will be discussed later.**

【14】**1.7Summary： Prospect of neuropsychological testing of dementia**

【15】**As worldwide life expectancy raises， the upcoming decades will see a global increase in the number of patients with dementia. This will be accompanied by an enormous medical and psychosocial challenge for the patients， their relatives， and society. The diagnosis of dementia is a syndrome diagnosis and should therefore be based on accepted criteria (e.g.， the ICD-10). The syndrome of dementia can be caused by several diseases which must be dif-ferentiated. Only an etiological classification (e.g.， which is listed in ICD-10) permits a well-founded statement about disease progress and necessary treat-ment. Dementia is a clinical， descriptive diagnosis； it does not necessarily imply a prognostic statement and even if the cause is progressive neurode-generative the long-term course may vary considerably between patients.**

**Effective treatment for dementia relies on precise and early diagnosis because in later stages the neurodegenerative process already caused irrevers-ible atrophy. During later phases of dementia， delaying its progression will be the most important concern. There are currently no specific or clear-cut biomarkers for many types of dementia. Therefore the differential diagnosis relies on the clinical investigation of the patients and on the combination of different information to arrive at the most appropriate diagnosis (“probable”in the case of a combined positive functional and somatic validation and“possible”in the case of only the functional impairments coinciding with the diagnosis). Neuropsychological testing is one method that can assist the dif-ferential diagnosis of dementia at the earliest clinical period of the disease. While screening tests like the MMSE help in determining the severity of the dementia， they do not provide information for a differential diagnosis， or do they detect the first signs of cognitive decline. Moreover， most of the screen-ing tests do not rely heavily enough on age-， gender-， and education-based test norms. Because these variables influence the results of screening tests， these tests do not convey reliable information. Rather， they provide only an estimation of the disease’s progression. Such a rating is important to judge the probable handicaps of the patient in everyday life and to assist the|删除0换行|decision-making process regarding， for example， driving or nursing homes. Neuropsychological testing in patients with suspected dementia therefore has two purposes： predicting the ability to live independently and to offer infor-mation about the possible cause of the impairment (supporting a specific dif-ferential diagnosis). Hopefully in the near future， there will be a third purpose of neuropsychological testing： to inform patients about the best func-tional treatment as well as its optimal level of difficulty (the scarce literature concerning neuropsychological rehabilitation in the specific dementias will be discussed at the end of the following chapters).**

【17】With respect to the purpose of differential diagnosis， Table 1.14 provides an overview of a set of core tests that may be used for a first impression of the cognitive problems. These core tests should be complemented by further tests depending on the etiological hypothesis based on this assessment.

【18】**The CERAD-NAB is a standardized test battery that is based on the results of more than 1100 control subjects  and there-fore the use of the CERAD-NAB as a core set of tests is recommended. In theory， a performance below an absolute cut-off score should be indicative of the specific neurodegenerative disease the patient is suffering from. Unfortunately， there seems to be no absolute cut-off scores for any subtest of the CERAD-NAB concerning differential diagnosing.**

【19】**The statement of a possible diagnosis depends on the formulation of assumptions regarding the kind of disease that might be present. Such assumptions depend on the anamnesis， which should encompass questions concerning cognitive deficits as well as autonomous functioning， walking， control of the hands， mood， and previous relevant diseases of the patient and their relatives. Together with the results of the CERAD-NAB and the other tests from the core set， it should be possible to define specific impairment patterns that help to develop a hypothesis for the differential diagnosis. This**

Therefore a neuropsychological differential diagnosis must be based on a combination of standard tests and a flexible integration of more specific ones. In the following chapters， we will analyze which additional tests best assist the differential diagnosis of a variety of different dementias.**

【22】**The test core test set defined earlier should be used in patients older than60 years. In younger patients， especially in those that are well-functioning the set of tests might be too easy and therefore not sensitive enough for sub-tle impairments. 【74】**Most textbooks consider the causes of red eye to be con-junctivitis， iritis， or glaucoma， but it may be the result of taking the night plane from Los Angeles to New York. The cornea may be involved by a foreign body or keratitis； corneal ulcers should also be looked for. Proceeding to deeper layers， the physician should consider iritis， scle-ritis， or injury to these structures. Finally， between the cornea and iris is the canal of Schlemm， which recalls glaucoma. The vascular supply suggests a cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Another method that will bring to mind even more of the possibilities is to use the mnemonic FOREIGN. The word and the first letter signify foreign bodies. The O sug-gests otolaryngologic conditions such as upper respiratory infections. The R brings to mind refractive errors and astig-matism. 【78】Pinning down the diagnosis of a red eye is usually not dif-ficult because most causes will be evident to the naked eye. Even when conjunctivitis is likely， always check the visual acuity in the affected eye to rule out a more serious condition. However， a careful search for a foreign body with a magnify-ing glass and for a comeal abrasion using fluorescein will be necessary in some cases. The association of other signs and symptoms will be invaluable. A child with red eyes and cer-vical lymphadenopathy may have Kawasaki disease. Diffuse erythema of the eye usually indicates trauma， conjunctivitis， or scleritis， whereas circumcorneal injection suggests iritis or glaucoma. Episcleritis is a focal erythema that fails to blanch with one drop of phenylephrine 2.5%. A dilated pupil sug-gests glaucoma， whereas a constricted or distorted pupil sug-gests iritis. A slit lamp will differentiate keratitis and obscure foreign bodies. Tonometry is useful in differentiating glau-coma from other conditions. Acute closed angle glaucoma is associated with nausea， vomiting， and halos and is a medi-cal emergency. A smear and culture will help differentiate infectious conjunctivitis from allergic conjunctivitis， but the latter is usually bilateral whereas the former is usually unilat-eral. An ophthalmologist should be consulted immediately if there is any doubt about the diagnosis.

【69】**This condition is being discussed in this section because the thorax is the most common region for it to make itself felt. It occurs much more commonly in the older person than the younger. Both sexes are equally affected， and no immunity is granted by an attack.**

【112】**The Lumbar Spine**

【113】**The lumbar spine and the neck are the two most common spinal regions treated by the generalist orthopedic therapist. Unlike neck pain， most low back pain is nontraumatically induced. As elsewhere in the spine， a multitude of tissues have the potential for being painful when pro-voked appropriately. In the lumbar spine， there is either experimental and/or clinical evidence for the disks， zygapophyseal joints， muscles， ligaments， and dural sleeve as pain sources.**

【114】**Disk herniations causing neurological deficits seem to be seen more commonly here than in the cervical spine， possibly in part because of the increased stress on the lumbar disk and also because of the differ-ent ways in which the two disks degenerate. The lumbar disk retaining its， albeit drier， nucleus into old age whereas the cervical disk’s nucleus disappears at all but the lowest level by the middle twenties.**

【115】**Anatomically， the areas are distinct： The spinal cord inhabits the cer-vical spine canal whereas the cauda equina， the cord terminating at about the first lumbar level， inhabits the lumbar spine. This means that a cer-vical posterior disk herniation compressing the contents of the spinal canal may cause an upper motor lesion， whereas in the lumbar spine the result will most frequently be a lower motor lesion. This compression of the cauda equina is the most frequent pathology in the lumbar spine. There are no uncovertebral or costovertebral joints ta protect the inter-vertebral canal and its contents from disk compression as there are in the cervical and thoracic regions. Certainly the cervical disk and possi-bly the thoracic disk are radically different from their lumbar counter-parts in makeup.**

**However， with all of this concentration on the lumbar disk as a source of disability， it should be realized that symptomatic externalization of|删除0换行|the disk is considered by mosi authorities to be a rare occurrence， pos-sibly being responsible for only about 5% of cases of low back pain.**

【117】**Serious Pathology**

【118】**Given the possibility of cancer in younger and older populations， age must be considered from the perspective of disk degradation. The older patient is also less likely to have a disk herniation because the disk has been successfully tested without previous failure over its lifetime and the person is generally putting less adverse stress on the disk because activity levels tend to drop with age. In addition， degenerative changes have made the spine and the disk stiffer， with changes in the zy-gapophyseal joints and in the disk itself. The possibility of metastatic disease must always be considered because 20% of spinal metastases occur in the lumbar spine. It is very unusual for the young patient， say up to about the middle twenties， to suffer from symptoms of a disk her-niation because it usually takes some time for nontraumatic degradative processes to superimpose themselves on the degenerative changes. How-ever， exceptions do occur. Recent literature gives the age of 9 years as the youngest patient age with established lumbar disk herniation.**

【119】**In the younger patient with acute low back pain， neoplastic disease should be considered first. One study looked at the clinical differences between children suffering from disk herniations and those with spinal tumors of all types. Spinal neoplastic disease in children tends to affect both legs， whereas disk herniations in the same group mainly affect one leg. Abdominal pain may be present in the neoplastic disorder and is usually absent in disk lesions. Neurological deficits are more commonly caused by neoplasms than by disk hemiations in this age group. The study also found that the younger the child， the greater the likelihood that neoplastic disease is the cause of the symptoms. Most of the chil-dren in the neoplastic group were under 10 years of age.**

【120】**As far as an upper age limit is concerned， I have seen a 65-year-old woman with acute articular signs， radicular pain， segmental sensory loss， and weakness that imaging studies subsequently confirmed as a fifth lumbar disk herniation with first sacral nerve compression. The litera-ture offers examples of patients over 70 years of age with disk hernia-tion. However， the pathology seems to differ from that found in patients less than 60 years old. In the patient over 60， the nucleus does not ap-pear to be a major factor in the condition. The main pathology is anu-lar sequestration or avulsion of the cartilaginous end-plate， which then herniates posteriorly with the anulus. It must be remembered that disk herniation in both the young and older populations is an oddity， and other causes of disklike signs and symptoms must be considered and excluded before accepting the diagnosis of disk herniation.**

【121】**Intervertebral Disk Pathologies**

【122】**There are various ways of classifying disk lesions， based on the size， the location， or the composition of the herniated material. The classical method of quantifying disk lesions is based on the size of the external-ization and the material that has hemiated as follows'：**

【123】**_I.Protrusion._ This is a relatively small bulge on the disk with no migration of nuclear material. It may be caused by a weakness in the anulus， possibly the result of the alignment of circumferential fissures or a radial tear. There are biomechanical effects but often no dural or neural compromise.**

【124】**_2\. Prolapse.There is migration of the nucleus， but it is constrained_ by the anulus and is not externalized. The bulge is much larger， and if it is a clinical rather than an imaging entity， dural and neural signs can be expected. Of the movements， flexion tends to provoke pain more than extension， and the patient has trouble sitting and bending.**

【125】**_3\. Extrusion._ The nuclear material has become externalized， and the pressure effect is much larger than the prolapse. Neurological deficit can be expected. All movements tend to reproduce the pain， and the patient is uncomfortable with both flexion and extension activities and postures. There is often deformity in the form of kyphosis combined with straight deviation or with scoliosis.**

【126】**_4\. Sequestration.The extruded nuclear material has fragmented and_ lies in the spinal canal. The effects of this condition depend on the sizes of the fragments and their locations.**

【127】**This classical categorization based mainly on nuclear migration has recently been challenged. The concept of disk degeneration being a pathological process that is of itself painful has been questioned for quite some time. Certainly， common sense would dictate that if degeneration of the spinal segment were painful then almost everybody would be painful all of the time， as this is an almost universal and nonreversible process.**
